newsitem.title: UK: Redwood, Howard join race to succeed UK's Major.
newsitem.headline: Redwood, Howard join race to succeed UK's Major.

text.p: Two former cabinet ministers from the right wing of Britain's opposition Conservative Party joined the battle to succeed John Major as leader on Tuesday and a third was on the brink of declaring himself a candidate.

After the party's election rout by the Labour Party, former interior minister Michael Howard and leading Eurosceptic John Redwood said they would take on fellow right-winger Peter Lilley and pro-European Kenneth Clarke, finance minister under Major.

Former Welsh Secretary William Hague, a youthful 36 and already the bookmakers' favourite, was expected to make his candidacy public on Wednesday after having second thoughts and pulling out of an agreement with Howard not to stand.

The Conservatives, who had been in power for the past 18 years, were reduced to a rump of 165 MPs in the 659-seat parliament at last week's election as Tony Blair led his Labour Party to its biggest victory in history.
Major, crushed at the end of six years as Prime Minister, immediately decided to step down as leader but will stay on until a successor is chosen.

Redwood and Howard stressed the enormity of the task that the new Conservative leader will face, Howard calling it "formidable" and Redwood, who unsuccessfully challenged Major for the leadership in 1995, "awesome".

They stressed the need for party unity, especially on the vexed issue of Britain's relations with Europe, a running sore in the party for at least four years before the election. "I don't want a sectional party, a factional party, a party obsessed by only one issue," said Redwood. "The Conservative Party is a broad church. It must stay as a broad church. The trouble is we don't have enough worshippers at the moment."
"We must give the parliamentary party clear, principled direction and strong leadership around which all can unite," Howard told a news conference.
But Howard was forced to admit that his initial initiative to establish a measure of unity had broken down.
He confirmed media reports that he and Hague reached a pact on Monday night which was sealed in a toast of champagne.
Under the accord, Howard would have stood for the leadership and, if successful, made Hague, 20 years his junior, his deputy. Overnight, the agreement had broken down.

"An agreement was reached with Mr Hague. He had second thoughts. He was certainly entitled to have second thoughts," Howard said. Before Blair became Labour leader in 1994, his debates with Howard on home affairs were one of the parliamentary highlights.

Redwood said he was well placed to provide leadership for the fight-back because he had been out of ministerial office for two years before the election -- he resigned as Welsh Secretary in 1995 to challenge Major.
"Against (Prime Minister) Tony Blair across the despatch box, I would not have to defend every last deed of the 1992-7 government, and could look forward," he said.
In the 1995 contest, Redwood was well beaten by Major, who has led the party since replacing Margaret Thatcher in 1990.
After his defeat Redwood formed a right-wing think-tank and, although not openly attacking Major, continued to put forward his Eurosceptic views widely and openly.
With former Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine having ruled himself out of the race because of ill health, the bookmakers William Hill make Hague favourite to replace Major.
Hague, who is in the centre of the party, is quoted at 6-4, with Clarke second favourite at 4-1, Howard and Lilley at 9-2 and Redwood on 10-1.
